title: The Fensky Triangle
logline: Ted's first public commission is a bench on Fensky Triangle, facing eleven inches of the Hudson, and Zoey Pierson, whom he hasn't been in a room with in four years, is fighting to turn it toward the street for the eighty-four-year-old neighbor who watches the corner. Zoey recruits Lily, Ted keeps Marshall and Robin, Barney bills both sides by the hour, and a community board hearing in Ted's own lecture hall leaves the gang far more radicalized than the two people actually fighting.
coldOpen: Kids, I've designed towers, a museum and two bridges. But the angriest this city ever got at me was over six feet of oak. A bench. Facing the wrong way.

couch.line: A bench? That's the whole story?
Luke, some of the bloodiest wars in this city have been fought over where to sit.

guests.name: Vivian Castellano
guests.role: eighty-four, leader of the Lookouts, who has watched Fensky Triangle from a lawn chair every afternoon since 1971; scores every passerby out of ten, out loud, and is always three moves ahead of everyone in the room

guests.name: Bernadette Kowalczyk
guests.role: chair of the Community Board Two Parks Committee for twenty-six years; flat, unshockable, times every speaker, answers almost everything with 'Noted' and measures every dispute against the Great Hydrant Debate of 1994

scenes.summary: Ted unveils his first public commission: a bench on Fensky Triangle facing eleven inches of river, with a plaque. Nobody knows who Mortimer Fensky was. Zoey walks in; she and Ted haven't been in a room in four years (a flashback shows how 'civil' they've been). She's recruiting Ted's friends against the bench for the Lookouts. Lily defects, Marshall and Robin stay with Ted, Barney hires himself out to both sides. The hearing is in Ted's own lecture hall. Button: Robin reminds Ted how his last fight with Zoey went.

beats.line: In the fall of 2013, the City of New York gave me my first public commission.
Guys. You are looking at the architect of the city's newest public work.
A bridge? Tell me it's a bridge. Women love a man with a bridge.
It's a bench.
So, a bridge. But shorter. And for sitting. And not over anything.
A bench is architecture at its purest. A roof says, stay. A door says, leave. A bench says, sit with me.
And this booth says, Ted is about to show us slides.
It faces due west, toward the Hudson. You can see eleven inches of river. Twelve if you lean.
beats.title: The Fensky Triangle Bench, by Mosby Architects
lines: Six feet of reclaimed white oak
Cantilevered steel base, so it appears to float
Faces due west, toward the Hudson River

beats.line: Ted, eleven inches of river is just a puddle with a good agent.
It's framed between a parking garage and a dentist, Lily. It's a gallery.
Wait. Where's Fensky Triangle?
Bleecker and nowhere. Smallest park in the West Village. It's a traffic island with ambition.
Who's Fensky?
Nobody knows. The plaque just says Mortimer Fensky. No dates. No achievements. Not even a verb.
That's so sad. A guy did one thing once, and nobody wrote down what.
That will never be me. My bench gets a plaque.
He's had the font picked out since 2004.
Gill Sans. Humble, but confident.
Zoey.
Ted.
Four years. Should we leave? I feel like we should leave.
Marshall, if you move, I will end you.
Zoey and I have run into each other. Very civilly.
Kids, I want to be honest with you about how civil it was.
Marshall! Hey! Can't talk, I'm on the phone. With you. Bye!
Hi, Mom. Yes, I'm in a store. No, I'm leaving the store. Right now.
For the record, my call was real.
Your phone was upside down.
So was yours.
Relax, Ted. I'm not here for you. I'm here to recruit your friends.
The city is about to bolt a bench onto Fensky Triangle. Facing the wrong way.
It faces the Hudson!
It turns its back on a whole neighborhood to stare at eleven inches of New Jersey.
That's river. New Jersey starts at twelve.
Since 1971, a group of neighbors has sat on that triangle every afternoon. In lawn chairs. Facing the street.
They're called the Lookouts. They know every kid on Bleecker by name. They've stopped two bike thefts and one terrible perm.
So they turn their lawn chairs around.
Vivian Castellano is eighty-four with a brand-new hip, Ted. She is not turning around for New Jersey.
Lily. The Lookouts score everyone who walks past. Out of ten. Out loud.
I'm in.
Sorry, Ted. She said out loud.
Marshall, I need an environmental lawyer.
Zoey, Ted's my best friend. And I'm from Minnesota. Benches face water. It's in our state constitution.
Marshall.
Lily.
Robin?
A bench facing the street means strangers stare at you. I get stared at for a living. River.
And I am available to both sides. Three co-op boards, a zoning war, one very ugly parking space. Never lost.
Which side were you on?
Both. That's how I never lost.
Hearing's Thursday. Community Board Two. Their room flooded, so it moved to the university. Room three-eleven.
That's my lecture hall.
Then I'll see you on your turf, Professor.
Fine. She wants a fight? I've fought Zoey Pierson before.
And you lost.
I knocked down her building!
And then you dated her. That's losing twice.

scenes.summary: The Community Board hearing in Ted's lecture hall. The gang shows up in team colors. Chair Bernadette times everyone. Vivian scores Ted a four. Marshall's records request on Fensky turns up one circular index card (Vivian looks smug). Lily has turned the marital bed to face the street; Robin's 'objective' segment is called Face the River, New York; Barney testifies for both sides and bills by the hour. Ted and Zoey fall into their old war. Bernadette orders them to agree on one bench by next Thursday, or it faces a wall.

beats.line: I'd taught in that lecture hall for three years. I had never once filled it.
Community Board Two, Parks Committee, is in session. Item one. A bench.
Two minutes per speaker. No chanting. And Vivian, no scoring the speakers.
You're a five, Bernadette.
Noted.
The architect. Two minutes.
Thank you, Madam Chair. Hi, I'm Ted Mosby, architect—
One fifty.
A bench should face something larger than ourselves. The river was here before us. It will be here after us.
Larger than ourselves? It's eleven inches, Ted. Vivian's bigger than that, and she's four foot ten.
Four eleven.
Madam Chair, a bench shouldn't face something eternal. It should face something that waves back.
The river waves.
Mrs. Castellano. Two minutes.
I don't need two minutes. I need one look at him.
I know you. Ten after eight, every morning. Scarf. Face like a sad poem.
The Lookouts score everybody who passes. Out loud. I brought the book.
The hat girl, nine. The big sweet one, eight. The dentist, seven. You, four.
beats.title: The Lookouts: Official Scores, Fensky Triangle

beats.line: A four?
Five in the red boots. The boots are the only thing in your life that's committed.
The big sweet one. That's me, right? Lily, am I the big sweet one?
You were. Before you chose the river.
Excuse me. Where's Barney Stinson on that chart?
Two a.m., Fridays, different girl every week. I don't score you. I pray for you.
Madam Chair, I filed a records request on Mortimer Fensky. So nobody can claim this triangle has history.
And?
The city's entire file is one index card. It says, see Fensky, Mortimer.
So I flipped it over. It says, see front.
Madam Chair, as a proud member of the Lookouts—
You've been a Lookout for four days!
And I've scored three hundred people! The doorman is a three!
Let the record show my wife has turned our bed around. To face the street.
That's where the people are, Marshall!
It faces the bathroom!
Madam Chair. Robin Scherbatsky, Metro News One. I've covered this story every night. Objectively.
Your segment is called Face the River, New York.
That's a coincidence.
Madam Chair, I rise on behalf of the street.
Mr. Stinson, you rose on behalf of the river twenty minutes ago.
And I made some excellent points. Now watch me destroy them.
Your tie is river. Your vest is street.
I dress for my clients. They both pay by the hour, so honestly, take your time.
You always do this. You find one sweet old lady and you hide behind her.
I'm not hiding behind her, Ted. She's load-bearing.
This is the Arcadian all over again!
Last time, you won! And what did you win? Me! And look how that went!
Agreed!
Agreed!
Noted.
Twenty-six years I've chaired this committee. In ninety-four, we had a hydrant. Two divorces, and a man moved to Delaware.
You two. The architect and the hat. Sit down together, agree on one bench, and bring it back Thursday.
And if we can't?
Then the bench faces north.
What's north?
A wall.

scenes.summary: Ted and Zoey meet on neutral ground at Lucarelli's. The gang arrives as 'observers' in team colors and are far worse than the principals: Lily scores Ted out loud, Marshall slept facing west, Lily rates the mailman, Robin defends her eleven inches. Ted and Zoey realize their seconds are worse than they ever were, and throw them out. Alone, Zoey admits she doesn't know what they are when they aren't fighting or dating; Vivian got her through her divorce. Ted admits he wanted the plaque. They become friends, Penny calls out 'Aunt Zoey', and Ted invents the conversation bench. Button: their friends will never accept it.

beats.line: We met at Lucarelli's on Carmine Street. Neutral ground. She'd picketed it in 2006. I'd been dumped in it in 2008.
So.
So.
You look formidable.
Thank you. You look like a four.
Ground rules. No architecture words.
Zoey, I can't even order without architecture words. The lasagna here is load-bearing.
What are you doing here?
Observing. The Lookouts sent me.
I brought a forty-page brief. Thirty of it is about sunsets.
And I'm observing for both sides. Separate invoices. Same hourly rate.
Zoey. Score him out loud. It rattles them.
Lily, I'm not going to—
Four!
No coaching across the aisle, Marshall. You slept on the couch.
Facing west! With dignity!
Lily, you gave our mailman a two.
He's been a two for six years, Robin! Somebody had to say it out loud!
You've changed, Lily.
Vivian gave me a lawn chair, Robin. It has my name on it.
Marshall and I watch the sunset from that triangle every night. It's the best eleven inches of my week.
That's what she—
Barney!
Were we this bad?
We were worse. You made a slideshow about my hat.
It was a presentation. A slideshow doesn't have a narrative arc.
Okay. Everybody out.
We have a right to observe!
Lily, go home. Score the doorman.
He's a three.
I'm billing you both for the walk to the door.
Do you want to know why I haven't been in a room with you for four years?
Because I knocked down your building?
Because when we're not fighting and we're not dating, I have no idea what we are.
Me neither. So why this bench, Zoey? Why do you care this much?
After my divorce, I sat on that triangle every afternoon. Vivian never asked me a single question.
She just scored strangers out loud until I laughed. It took her eleven days.
I wanted the plaque. I didn't want to end up a Mortimer Fensky. A name nobody can explain.
Ted, nobody remembers the plaque. They remember who was sitting there.
I've missed this.
Arguing?
Losing to you. Nobody else does it right. Marshall agrees with everything I say about cornices.
Everyone I know either agrees with me or calls the police.
So if we're not enemies, and we're not—
Friends, Ted. It's when you lose the argument and still split the fries.
Wait. Aunt Zoey? The one who chained herself to my school's vending machine?
She was right about that vending machine, Penny.
Wait. What if it faces both ways?
A bench can't face both ways.
A conversation bench can. An S-curve. One seat faces the river. One seat faces the street.
And the two people sitting on it?
Face each other.
That's your first good idea since the boots.
The gang will be relieved. They just want this to be over.
Ted. Robin has a segment. Barney has invoices. And Lily has a lawn chair with her name on it.

scenes.summary: Second hearing. Ted and Zoey present the conversation bench together. The radicalized gang rejects it; Barney's both-sides scheme dies because Ted and Zoey compared invoices. Lily calls on Vivian to back the street, and Vivian takes the half: she only watches one thing, the bodega, where her husband Mortimer Fensky, very much alive, works the register. He named the triangle by writing his own name in box seven of a 1974 lawn chair permit. He waves at her every day. Approved. Lily and Marshall reconcile, Vivian upgrades Ted to a six, and Zoey's first act as a friend is to critique his font. Future Ted: the plaque says Vivian Castellano.

beats.line: Community Board Two, Parks Committee. Item one. Still the bench.
Architect. Hat. Do we have an agreement?
We do.
Together.
A conversation bench. An S-curve. One seat faces the river.
One seat faces the street.
And the two people sitting on it face each other.
Absolutely not.
Half a river? Ted, I've done nine segments on this!
I slept on a couch for this!
Madam Chair, my clients reject this compromise. Both of them. Separately. At my hourly rate.
Your clients compared invoices, Barney.
Friends do that.
Friends? You can't be friends! I put a deposit on a jet ski!
Vivian. Tell them. The street deserves the whole bench.
I'll take it.
What?
I only need one seat, dear. I only ever look at one thing.
The kids on Bleecker?
The bodega. Morty works the register.
Who's Morty?
Mortimer Fensky. My husband.
Mortimer Fensky is alive?
He's at the bodega. He's been at that register since gas was forty cents.
In 1974, he applied for a permit for my lawn chair. Box seven said, name of park. He wrote his own name.
Noted.
Forty years I've faced that bodega. And forty years, every customer, he looks up and waves at me.
He waves, Lily. Mortimer Fensky got a verb.
Also, he owes me eleven dollars. Somebody has to keep an eye on him.
The conversation bench is approved. This committee has never been more tired.
Marshmallow. Come home. You can have the window side.
Lilypad, the window side faces the street.
I know.
For the record, Face the River, New York is not cancelled. It's getting a spin-off.
So, Mrs. Castellano. Am I still a four?
Six.
Six!
Stand next to a nine long enough, anybody goes up.
And as your friend? Gill Sans on the plaque is a little smug.
It's humble, but confident!
It's a four.
Kids, that bench is still there. Every Thursday, your Aunt Zoey sits across from me and tells me I'm wrong.
As for my plaque, Vivian filled out the dedication form herself. Box seven. It says Vivian Castellano. In Gill Sans.
